Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, yet its delivery remains constrained by variable efficacy, acute and prolonged toxicities, and complex manufacturing logistics. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across the CAR-T continuum at three distinct levels of evidentiary maturity. Externally validated parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data including CAR-HEMATOTOX, endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) and m-EASIX, MyCARe, and gradient-boosting cytokine release syndrome predictors provide deployable risk stratification today. Methodologically sophisticated tools using deep-learning positron emission tomography (PET) segmentation, attention-based digital-pathology analysis, and multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and circulating tumor DNA features have demonstrated technical promise but generally lack the multi-center external validation required for clinical-grade deployment. Forward-looking applications, including digital-twin frameworks, large language models, and closed-loop adaptive therapy, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. Conclusion
AI is being applied across the CAR-T continuum in three substantively different ways, and the maturity of each application differs sharply. First, parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data—CAR-HEMATOTOX, EASIX and its variants, gradient-boosting CRS predictors, infection-vs.-CRS triage classifiers, and disease-specific relapse indices—have been externally and prospectively validated across multi-center cohorts in LBCL, B-ALL, and MM. These tools are deployable today and provide interpretable, auditable decision support for clinicians managing the acute and subacute toxicities of CAR-T. They are the current evidence base, and they should be the operational starting point for any CAR-T program adopting AI. Second, more methodologically sophisticated tools, such as DL PET segmentation, attention-based WSI analysis, multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and ctDNA features, and the manufacturing-floor AI used for in-process quality control, have demonstrated strong technical performance but generally lack the cross-center external validation that characterizes the laboratory-based scoring systems. In their current state, these tools function best as upstream feature extractors that improve the input quality of more mature classical prediction systems, rather than as standalone clinical instruments. Their maturation pathway is clear: harmonized data substrates from registry consortia, federated training pipelines that respect institutional data ownership, and validation studies designed around the TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI reporting standards. Third, the genuinely forward-looking applications, such as digital twins, LLMs, closed-loop adaptive therapy, and integrative AI-nano-immune frameworks, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. We have addressed these in a dedicated “
outlook: Emerging and aspirational directions
” section so that they are not confused with current practice. The realistic horizon for any of them entering routine CAR-T workflows is measured in years and is gated by the same infrastructure constraints—shared registries, federated learning, FAIR-aligned governance, and drift monitoring—that limit the second tier. Methods

This study evaluates six machine learning models-Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, AdaBoost, Elastic Net, and Linear Regression to identify the most accurate algorithm for predicting mathematics performance among students from six high-performing East Asian countries/economies participating in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022. Affective, behavioral, and instructional factors consistently outperformed structural and socioeconomic variables in predictive importance.

Discussion and conclusion

These findings underscore the central role of student-proximal determinants in mathematics achievement within Confucian Heritage Culture educational contexts.
